raw_response:
I farm 12 mu in Quzhou, and on this land I will still run the wheat-maize rotation the way that has paid for me before, just a bit tighter on timing and a bit more exact on fertilizer. I have enough years in the field to know I should not start from zero every spring. I start from what worked last year, then I adjust for water, fertilizer price, and what kind of stand I want. With well irrigation in Quzhou, I will push wheat a little harder than dryland people do, because if wheat loses tillers in spring, that yield does not come back easily. On wheat I will use improved seed, rotary till after maize, put most phosphorus in the base fertilizer, keep potassium in but not too high, and split nitrogen so I do not waste too much before jointing. I will plan on 3 irrigations for wheat: one winter water if the soil is short of moisture, one at jointing, and one around booting or filling depending on the year. For maize, I will use a hybrid and keep the usual local wheat-stubble sowing system. I do that because it saves labor, catches moisture, and on 12 mu I care about efficiency. I will not cut fertilizer too hard on maize, because losing an ear for the sake of saving a little fertilizer is not worth it. I will hold phosphorus lower than wheat, keep potassium steady, and leave enough nitrogen for the big bell stage. With my water access, I will plan on 2 irrigations for maize, mainly around seedling establishment if it is dry and again near tasseling or grain fill if rain does not come. For pesticides, I will not spray by habit alone, but in a normal year I will count on about 3 passes on wheat and 2 on maize, because rust, aphids, weeds, and then corn borer or leaf disease can all cost real grain. On yield, I will aim for about 600 kg per mu on wheat and 650 kg per mu on maize. That is not bragging yield, but on this land with water and careful timing, it is a solid target that pays.
